## Question

Genes whose local network wiring is similar, measured by their graphlet degree vectors
(signatures), tend to share biological function [@milenkovic2008]. Gene co-expression
networks, however, are usually made by thresholding correlations which treats
every kept edge as certain and every other pair as absent. Probabilistic graphlets
[@doriabelenguer2020] keep each edge's probability instead but the original work used raw
scores as probabilities and found no gain for co-expression networks. 

Here I ask:

> Do graphlet features from a **calibrated** probabilistic co-expression network predict
> gene function better than graphlet features from **binary** networks made from the same
> data?

## Data

Single-cell RNA-seq of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 8 donors with lupus
[@kang2018; GEO GSE96583, batch 2]. I use the unstimulated, singlet CD14+ monocytes:
`{python} f"{int(size.cells):,}"` cells after quality control, from
`{python} int(size.donors)` donors and `{python} f"{int(size.genes):,}"` genes (detected in
at least 10 % of cells, most variable, no mitochondrial or ribosomal genes).
Gene function labels are Gene Ontology biological process terms [@ashburner2000]
(release 2026-08-05, evidence codes IEA, ND and IEP excluded):
`{python} f"{go.genes_with_BP_annotation:,}"` of the genes are annotated, and
`{python} int(go.terms_used)` terms with `{python} go.term_size_range` genes are used.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-donors

d = donors.rename(columns={"ind": "Donor", "cells": "Cells"})
d["Donor"] = d["Donor"].astype(int).astype(str)
Markdown(d.to_markdown(index=False))
```

## Methods

1. **Edge stability.** 
   Cells were resampled with replacement within each donor 100 times,
   summed into metacells of 10 cells and gene–gene Pearson correlations computed. A pair
   counts as co-expressed in a resample if its correlation is at least
   τ = `{python} f"{edges.tau:.3f}"` (the 99th percentile of all pairs in the full data).
   Stability is the fraction of resamples in which a pair is co-expressed, computed on all
   donors and separately on two halves of four donors.
2. **Calibration.** 
   Stability in one half of the donors was mapped, by isotonic
   regression, to whether the pair is co-expressed in the *other* half. The edge
   probability *p* is the probability that the association replicates in independent
   donors. Pairs never co-expressed in any resample get *p* = 0 (see
   `docs/decisions.md`).
3. **Networks.** 
   The *probabilistic* network keeps every pair with *p* ≥ 0.01 and its
   probability. The *matched* binary network keeps the top pairs by *p*, as many as the
   probabilistic network's expected number of edges, so the two differ only in discarding
   uncertainty. The *naive* binary network keeps pairs with full-data correlation ≥ τ.
4. **Graphlets.** 
   Graphlet degree vectors (orbits 0–14) were counted with ORCA for the
   binary networks and expected counts for the probabilistic network were estimated from
   `{python} int(mc.realizations)` sampled realisations.
5. **Function prediction.** 
   For each GO term, logistic regression was trained on each
   feature set (log-transformed, standardised) and scored by the area under the
   precision–recall curve (AUPR) in 5-fold cross-validation repeated 3 times, with the same
   folds for every feature set. Baselines: expected degree only and expression only
   (three summary statistics and 20 principal components). Feature sets were compared per
   term with the paired Wilcoxon test and Benjamini–Hochberg correction.

## Results

### Calibration

```{python}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Reliability of edge scores, out of sample: the score of a gene pair in one half of the donors against how often the pair is co-expressed in the other half. Points on the dashed line are perfectly calibrated."
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of observed replication rate against predicted probability, with a dashed diagonal for perfect calibration. Raw bootstrap stability (orange circles, solid line) lies far below the diagonal: pairs with high stability replicate much less often than their stability suggests. Calibrated probabilities (blue squares, dashed line) only reach about 0.45 and lie much nearer the diagonal: at 0.34 and 0.44 they replicate about 28 and 32 percent of the time, though the lowest bins scatter between 2 and 7 percent."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ls=":", color="grey", lw=1, label="perfect calibration")
for label, colour, marker, ls in (("raw stability", "#D55E00", "o", "-"), ("calibrated p", "#0072B2", "s", "--")):
    r = rel[rel.score == label]
    ax.plot(r.mean_score, r.observed, marker=marker, ls=ls, color=colour, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted probability of replication")
ax.set_ylabel("Observed replication in the other donors")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Raw stability is over-confident: pairs found in almost every resample replicate in
the other donors only about a quarter of the time. Calibrated probabilities are much
closer to the observed replication but never exceed about 0.45, so no pair is more
likely than not to replicate (@fig-calibration). The Brier score (mean squared error of
the probabilities, lower is better) falls from `{python} f"{brier.brier_raw_stability.mean():.3f}"` to
`{python} f"{brier.brier_calibrated.mean():.3f}"` on average over the two directions.

### Networks

```{python}
#| label: tbl-networks
#| tbl-cap: "The three networks. For the probabilistic network, edges are candidate pairs with p ≥ 0.01 and expected edges is the sum of their probabilities."
n = nets.copy()
n["network"] = n["network"].map({"probabilistic": "Probabilistic", "binary_matched": "Binary, matched density",
                                 "binary_naive_r": "Binary, naive (r ≥ τ)"})
n = n[["network", "genes_with_edges", "edges", "expected_edges", "mean_degree"]]
n.columns = ["Network", "Genes with edges", "Edges", "Expected edges", "Mean degree"]
Markdown(n.to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=",.0f", intfmt=","))
```

Of `{python} f"{int(edges.pairs):,}"` gene pairs, `{python} f"{int(edges.pairs_stability_gt0):,}"`
were co-expressed in at least one resample. The matched binary network has the same
expected number of edges as the probabilistic network
(`{python} f"{int(round(prob_net.expected_edges)):,}"`) but reaches only
`{python} f"{int(matched_net.genes_with_edges):,}"` of the `{python} f"{int(size.genes):,}"`
genes (@tbl-networks).

### Function prediction

```{python}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Prediction of GO biological process terms by each feature set: median and mean AUPR over terms, median AUPR relative to random (the term's share of genes) and the share of terms predicted better than random."
s = summary[["median_AUPR", "mean_AUPR", "median_fold_enrichment_over_random", "terms_better_than_random_%", "median_AUROC"]]
s = s.sort_values("median_AUPR", ascending=False).reset_index()
s.columns = ["Features", "Median AUPR", "Mean AUPR", "Median × random", "Terms > random (%)", "Median AUROC"]
Markdown(s.to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=".3f"))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-aupr
#| fig-cap: "AUPR relative to random for every GO term and feature set (log scale). Boxes show the median and quartiles, the dashed line is random guessing."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal box plots of AUPR fold enrichment over random, one box per feature set, on a log scale from about 0.8 to 20, with a dashed vertical line at 1 for random guessing. Expression only and probabilistic GDV have the highest medians, both a little above 2; the two binary GDV sets are near 1.9 and degree only is lowest near 1.6. All boxes lie mostly to the right of the random line."
order = summary.sort_values("median_AUPR").index.tolist()
data = [pred.loc[pred.features == f, "aupr_fold_enrichment"].values for f in order]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.boxplot(data, orientation="horizontal", tick_labels=order, showfliers=False, widths=0.6)
ax.axvline(1, ls="--", color="grey", lw=1)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("AUPR ÷ random (log scale)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-paired
#| fig-cap: "AUPR of each GO term with probabilistic graphlets against matched-density binary graphlets. Points above the diagonal are terms where probabilistic graphlets do better."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of 702 GO terms, AUPR with binary matched-density graphlets on the x axis and with probabilistic graphlets on the y axis, both on log scales from about 0.01 to 0.4, with a dashed diagonal. About three quarters of the points lie above the diagonal, most of them close to it, showing that probabilistic graphlets give a somewhat higher AUPR for most terms."
w = pred.pivot(index="term", columns="features", values="aupr")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4.5))
ax.scatter(w[MATCHED], w[PROB], s=8, alpha=0.5, color="#0072B2")
lim = [w[[MATCHED, PROB]].min().min() * 0.9, w[[MATCHED, PROB]].max().max() * 1.1]
ax.plot(lim, lim, ls="--", color="grey", lw=1)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel(f"AUPR, {MATCHED}"); ax.set_ylabel(f"AUPR, {PROB}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Probabilistic graphlets against each other feature set, paired over GO terms: median difference in AUPR, share of terms where probabilistic graphlets do better and the Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected Wilcoxon q-value."
t = tests[["comparison", "terms", "median_AUPR_difference", "probabilistic_wins_%", "BH_q"]].copy()
t["comparison"] = t["comparison"].str.replace(f"{PROB} vs ", "", regex=False)
t["BH_q"] = t["BH_q"].map(lambda q: "< 0.0001" if q < 1e-4 else f"{q:.4f}")
t.columns = ["Probabilistic GDV vs", "Terms", "Median AUPR difference", "Probabilistic better (%)", "q"]
Markdown(t.to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=".4f"))
```

Probabilistic graphlets predict GO terms better than binary graphlets from the same data
at the same expected density: median AUPR `{python} f"{summary.loc[PROB, 'median_AUPR']:.3f}"`
against `{python} f"{summary.loc[MATCHED, 'median_AUPR']:.3f}"`, better on
`{python} f"{vs_matched['probabilistic_wins_%']:.0f}"` % of the
`{python} int(vs_matched.terms)` terms (@fig-paired, @tbl-tests). They also beat the
naive binary network and expected degree, but not the expression features themselves
(median AUPR `{python} f"{summary.loc['Expression only', 'median_AUPR']:.3f}"`; probabilistic
graphlets better on only `{python} f"{vs_expr['probabilistic_wins_%']:.0f}"` % of terms).

## Discussion

Once edge probabilities are calibrated and pairs with no evidence are given probability
zero, probabilistic graphlets capture gene function better than graphlets of thresholded
networks, unlike in the original study [@doriabelenguer2020]. The gains are moderate: all
methods are only about two to three times better than random and the expression profiles
from which the network is built remain the best predictor.

Limitations:

- Setting *p* = 0 for pairs never seen in any resample was decided after a first run, in
  which every pair received a small probability and probabilistic graphlets did slightly
  *worse* than binary ones. Both runs are reported in `docs/decisions.md`.
- The matched binary network leaves some genes without edges, while the probabilistic
  network reaches every gene, part of the gain may come from this coverage.
- One dataset, one cell type and one way of building the network.
